studies.title: Amygdala-frontal connectivity during emotion regulation.
studies.abstract: Successful control of affect partly depends on the capacity to modulate negative emotional responses through the use of cognitive strategies (i.e., reappraisal). Recent studies suggest the involvement of frontal cortical regions in the modulation of amygdala reactivity and the mediation of effective emotion regulation. However, within-subject inter-regional connectivity between amygdala and prefrontal cortex in the context of affect regulation is unknown. Here, using psychophysiological interaction analyses of functional magnetic resonance imaging data, we show that activity in specific areas of the frontal cortex (dorsolateral, dorsal medial, anterior cingulate, orbital) covaries with amygdala activity and that this functional connectivity is dependent on the reappraisal task. Moreover, strength of amygdala coupling with orbitofrontal cortex and dorsal medial prefrontal cortex predicts the extent of attenuation of negative affect following reappraisal. These findings highlight the importance of functional connectivity within limbic-frontal circuitry during emotion regulation.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract describes an original task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants and reports task-related amygdala–prefrontal functional connectivity predicting affect attenuation. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This paper reports a task-based fMRI study in which participants were explicitly instructed to use cognitive reappraisal to down-regulate negative affect elicited by visual stimuli (IAPS pictures). The methods describe block-wise Reappraise and Maintain conditions, online self-report ratings, and within-task contrasts including conjunctions ([Maintain > Baseline] AND [Reappraise > Baseline]) used to identify amygdala activation as well as task-dependent PPI contrasts (Reappraise > Maintain). Group-level, voxelwise analyses are reported with peak coordinates (e.g., left amygdala MNI −22,0,−22) and whole-brain PPI results (Table 1, figures). The study therefore meets inclusion criteria I5 (task-based fMRI), I6 (instructed emotion regulation — reappraisal), I7 (visual stimuli), I8 (eligible sample), I9 (within-task contrasts related to regulation), I10 (group-level whole-brain maps with peak coordinates), and I11 (results reported in tables/figures/text). No exclusion criteria are met (not only ROI/only connectivity-only; whole-brain task analyses are present). Full text appears complete.

studies.title: Yoga Practitioners Uniquely Activate the Superior Parietal Lobule and Supramarginal Gyrus During Emotion Regulation.
studies.abstract: Chronic stress contributes to both mental and physical illness. A high prevalence and cost of stress-related illnesses North America warrants investigation into alternative or complementary therapies which may help reduce adverse reactions to stressful stimuli. Emotion regulation is the process of monitoring and adjusting emotional responses to environmental stimuli and stressors. Individuals who participate in physical activity are less likely to have adverse responses to potentially stressful situations, potentially due to adaptions in emotion regulation. Yoga is a form of physical activity involving stretching exercises and meditation, that may lessen individuals' levels of stress and anxiety and improve emotion regulation. High-frequency heart rate variability (HF-HRV) is considered a measure of parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity during the emotion regulation. Measuring HRV and brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) offers a useful, noninvasive approach to evaluating "neurovisceral" components of emotion regulation. We aimed to determine whether yoga practitioners (YP) exhibit different patterns of brain activation compared to recreational athletes (RA) without current yoga experience, while viewing emotionally arousing visual stimuli. Our secondary aim was to examine potential differences across groups in HRV throughout the presentation of these stimuli. Analysis of fMRI data during exposure to emotion-evoking (EE) stimuli revealed that the YP group activated two unique brain areas, namely the superior parietal lobule and the supramarginal gyrus. These areas have been associated with attentional awareness and reduced egocentric bias, processes that have been implicated in emotion regulation by others. The RA group activated the inferior middle frontal cortex, an area associated with cognitive reappraisal during emotion regulation. The YP group also demonstrated a trend towards a higher ratio of low- to high-frequency HRV compared to the RA group. The present findings support the presence of experience-dependent neurovisceral mechanisms associated with emotion regulation. Individuals who practice yoga regulate their neurovisceral responses to potentially stressful external stimuli in a different manner than recreational athletes who do not engage in yoga practice. studies.title: Staying cool when things get hot: emotion regulation modulates neural mechanisms of memory encoding.
studies.abstract: During times of emotional stress, individuals often engage in emotion regulation to reduce the experiential and physiological impact of negative emotions. Interestingly, emotion regulation strategies also influence memory encoding of the event. Cognitive reappraisal is associated with enhanced memory while expressive suppression is associated with impaired explicit memory of the emotional event. However, the mechanism by which these emotion regulation strategies affect memory is unclear. We used event-related fMRI to investigate the neural mechanisms that give rise to memory formation during emotion regulation. Twenty-five participants viewed negative pictures while alternately engaging in cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, or passive viewing. As part of the subsequent memory design, participants returned to the laboratory two weeks later for a surprise memory test. Behavioral results showed a reduction in negative affect and a retention advantage for reappraised stimuli relative to the other conditions. Imaging results showed that successful encoding during reappraisal was uniquely associated with greater co-activation of the left inferior frontal gyrus, amygdala, and hippocampus, suggesting a possible role for elaborative encoding of negative memories. This study provides neurobehavioral evidence that engaging in cognitive reappraisal is advantageous to both affective and mnemonic processes.

studies.title: fMRI neurofeedback facilitates anxiety regulation in females with spider phobia.
studies.abstract: Spider phobics show an exaggerated fear response when encountering spiders. This fear response is aggravated by negative and irrational beliefs about the feared object. Cognitive reappraisal can target these beliefs, and therefore has a fear regulating effect. The presented study investigated if neurofeedback derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) would facilitate anxiety regulation by cognitive reappraisal, using spider phobia as a model of anxiety disorders. Feedback was provided based on activation in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and right insula, as indicators of engagement and regulation success, respectively.

studies.title: The common and distinct neural bases of affect labeling and reappraisal in healthy adults.
studies.abstract: Emotion regulation is commonly characterized as involving conscious and intentional attempts to change felt emotions, such as, for example, through reappraisal whereby one intentionally decreases the intensity of one's emotional response to a particular stimulus or situation by reinterpreting it in a less threatening way. However, there is growing evidence and appreciation that some types of emotion regulation are unintentional or incidental, meaning that affective modulation is a consequence but not an explicit goal. For example, affect labeling involves simply verbally labeling the emotional content of an external stimulus or one's own affective responses without an intentional goal of altering emotional responses, yet has been associated with reduced affective responses at the neural and experiential levels. Although both intentional and incidental emotional regulation strategies have been associated with diminished limbic responses and self-reported distress, little previous research has directly compared their underlying neural mechanisms. In this study, we examined the extent to which incidental and intentional emotion regulation, namely, affect labeling and reappraisal, produced common and divergent neural and self-report responses to aversive images relative to an observe-only control condition in a sample of healthy older adults (N = 39). Affect labeling and reappraisal produced common activations in several prefrontal regulatory regions, with affect labeling producing stronger responses in direct comparisons. Affect labeling and reappraisal were also associated with similar decreases in amygdala activity. Finally, affect labeling and reappraisal were associated with correlated reductions in self-reported distress. Together these results point to common neurocognitive mechanisms involved in affect labeling and reappraisal, supporting the idea that intentional and incidental emotion regulation may utilize overlapping neural processes.

studies.title: Sex-Specific Effects of Childhood Poverty on Neurocircuitry of Processing of Emotional Cues: A Neuroimaging Study.
studies.abstract: There is accumulating evidence on the negative impacts of childhood poverty on physical and mental health. Previous work has suggested hyperactive neural response to social fear cues, as well as impairment in neural regulatory functions. However, despite differences found between males and females in stress-related and anxiety disorders, possible sex-specific effects of poverty on emotional processing have not been explored.

studies.title: The role of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in the regulation of craving by reappraisal in smokers.
studies.abstract: Drug cues can induce craving for drugs of abuse. Dysfunctional regulation of emotion and motivation regarding rewarding objects appears to be an integral part of addiction. It has been found that cognitive strategies decreased the intensity of craving in addicts. Reappraisal strategy is a type of cognitive strategy that requires participants to reinterpret the meaning of an emotional situation. In addition, studies have found that activation of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) is associated with the selection and application of cognitive reappraisal. In present study, we sought to determine whether such cognitive regulation engages the dACC and improves inhibition of craving in smokers.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in smokers using cognitive reappraisal to regulate craving (emotion regulation). studies.title: Neural substrates of social emotion regulation: a FMRI study on imitation and expressive suppression to dynamic facial signals.
studies.abstract: Emotion regulation is crucial for successfully engaging in social interactions. Yet, little is known about the neural mechanisms controlling behavioral responses to emotional expressions perceived in the face of other people, which constitute a key element of interpersonal communication. Here, we investigated brain systems involved in social emotion perception and regulation, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 20 healthy participants. The latter saw dynamic facial expressions of either happiness or sadness, and were asked to either imitate the expression or to suppress any expression on their own face (in addition to a gender judgment control task). fMRI results revealed higher activity in regions associated with emotion (e.g., the insula), motor function (e.g., motor cortex), and theory of mind (e.g., [pre]cuneus) during imitation. Activity in dorsal cingulate cortex was also increased during imitation, possibly reflecting greater action monitoring or conflict with own feeling states. In addition, premotor regions were more strongly activated during both imitation and suppression, suggesting a recruitment of motor control for both the production and inhibition of emotion expressions. Expressive suppression (eSUP) produced increases in dorsolateral and lateral prefrontal cortex typically related to cognitive control. These results suggest that voluntary imitation and eSUP modulate brain responses to emotional signals perceived from faces, by up- and down-regulating activity in distributed subcortical and cortical networks that are particularly involved in emotion, action monitoring, and cognitive control.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Task-based fMRI with healthy human participants instructed to regulate (expressive suppression) and imitate emotional facial expressions while viewing dynamic visual stimuli; reports task-related brain activation. Meets I1–I4. No exclusion criteria met.

studies.title: Reappraising social emotions: the role of inferior frontal gyrus, temporo-parietal junction and insula in interpersonal emotion regulation.
studies.abstract: Previous studies have reported the effect of emotion regulation (ER) strategies on both individual and social decision-making, however, the effect of regulation on socially driven emotions independent of decisions is still unclear. In the present study, we investigated the neural effects of using reappraisal to both up- and down-regulate socially driven emotions. Participants played the Dictator Game (DG) in the role of recipient while undergoing fMRI, and concurrently applied the strategies of either up-regulation (reappraising the proposer's intentions as more negative), down-regulation (reappraising the proposer's intentions as less negative), as well as a baseline "look" condition. Results showed that regions responding to the implementation of reappraisal (effect of strategy, that is, "regulating regions") were the inferior and middle frontal gyrus, temporo parietal junction and insula bilaterally. Importantly, the middle frontal gyrus activation correlated with the frequency of regulatory strategies in daily life, with the insula activation correlating with the perceived ability to reappraise the emotions elicited by the social situation. Regions regulated by reappraisal (effect of regulation, that is, "regulated regions") were the striatum, the posterior cingulate and the insula, showing increased activation for the up-regulation and reduced activation for down-regulation, both compared to the baseline condition. When analyzing the separate effects of partners' behavior, selfish behavior produced an activation of the insula, not observed when subjects were treated altruistically. Here we show for the first time that interpersonal ER strategies can strongly affect neural responses when experiencing socially driven emotions. Clinical implications of these findings are also discussed to understand how the way we interpret others' intentions may affect the way we emotionally react.

studies.title: Visual Attention to Suffering After Compassion Training Is Associated With Decreased Amygdala Responses.
studies.abstract: Compassion meditation training is hypothesized to increase the motivational salience of cues of suffering, while also enhancing equanimous attention and decreasing emotional reactivity to suffering. However, it is currently unknown how compassion meditation impacts visual attention to suffering, and how this impacts neural activation in regions associated with motivational salience as well as aversive responses, such as the amygdala. Healthy adults were randomized to 2 weeks of compassion or reappraisal training. We measured BOLD fMRI responses before and after training while participants actively engaged in their assigned training to images depicting human suffering or non-suffering. Eye-tracking data were recorded concurrently, and we computed looking time for socially and emotionally evocative areas of the images, and calculated visual preference for suffering vs. non-suffering. Increases in visual preference for suffering due to compassion training were associated with decreases in the amygdala, a brain region involved in negative valence, arousal, and physiological responses typical of fear and anxiety states. This pattern was specifically in the compassion group, and was not found in the reappraisal group. In addition, compassion training-related increases in visual preference for suffering were also associated with decreases in regions sensitive to valence and empathic distress, spanning the anterior insula and orbitofrontal cortex (while the reappraisal group showed the opposite effect). Examining visual attention alone demonstrated that engaging in compassion in general (across both time points) resulted in visual attention preference for suffering compared to engaging in reappraisal. Collectively, these findings suggest that compassion meditation may cultivate visual preference for suffering while attenuating neural responses in regions typically associated with aversive processing of negative stimuli, which may cultivate a more equanimous and nonreactive form of attention to stimuli of suffering.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Task-based BOLD fMRI in healthy adults randomized to compassion vs reappraisal training; participants engaged in instructed emotion-regulation strategies while viewing suffering/non-suffering images; reports task-related neural activation (amygdala, insula, OFC). studies.title: Instructions matter: a comparison of baseline conditions for cognitive emotion regulation paradigms.
studies.abstract: The choice of a meaningful baseline condition is a crucial issue for each experimental design. In the case of cognitive emotion regulation, it is common to either let participants passively view emotional stimuli without any further specific instructions or to instruct them to actively attend to and permit any arising emotions, and to contrast one of these baseline conditions with a regulation condition. While the "view" strategy can be assumed to allow for a more spontaneous emotional response, the "permit" strategy may result in a more pronounced affective and cognitive response. As these conceptual differences may be associated with differences both in subjective emotional experience and neural activation, we compared these two common control conditions within a single functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) experiment, during which participants were instructed to either passively view a set of unpleasant and neutral pictures or to actively permit any emotions arising in response to the unpleasant pictures. Trial-by-trial ratings confirmed that participants perceived the unpleasant pictures as more arousing than the neutral pictures, but also indicated higher subjective arousal during the "permit negative" as compared to the "view negative" and "view neutral" conditions. While both the "permit negative" and "view negative" conditions led to increased activation of the bilateral amygdala when contrasted with the passive viewing of neutral pictures, activation in the left amygdala was increased in response to the "permit" instruction as compared to the "view" instruction for unpleasant pictures. The increase in amygdala activation in both the "permit" and "view" conditions renders both strategies as suitable baseline conditions for studies of cognitive emotion regulation. Conceptual and activation differences, however, indicate that these two variants are not exchangeable and should be chosen depending on the experimental context.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Task-based fMRI in human participants comparing emotion-regulation-related instructions (permit/accept vs view) during viewing of unpleasant and neutral visual stimuli; reports subjective ratings and task-related brain activation (amygdala). studies.title: Neural bases of reappraisal regulatory effect on negative emotion in high reappraisers.
studies.abstract: Previous studies have reported that individual differences in reappraisal use are associated with particular patterns of neural activity. We hypothesized that if 'high reappraisers' (individuals who use reappraisal well in a behavioral experiment) completed two training sessions, they would exhibit more reliable patterns of neural activity related to cognitive reappraisal. In the present study, 13 high reappraisers were selected from 27 healthy volunteers through an initial behavioral experiment (first training) followed by a functional MRI experiment (second training). Emotional images selected from the International Affective Picture System were used for both the behavioral and functional MRI sessions of the experiment. The behavioral results revealed that reappraisal reduced subjective unpleasantness. The functional MRI results revealed that the cognitive reappraisal used by high reappraisers decreased the activation of emotion-responsive regions, including the amygdala, insula, and cingulate gyrus, and increased the activation of regulation-related regions, including the inferior prefrontal cortex, orbital prefrontal cortex, and dorsal medial prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest the involvement of inferior orbital and dorsal medial prefrontal cortex in constructing reappraisal strategies that modulate activity in emotion-processing systems.

studies.abstract: Sleep restriction has been proposed to cause impaired emotional processing and emotional regulation by inhibiting top-down control from prefrontal cortex to amygdala. Forty-seven young (age 20-30) and 33 older (age 65-75) participants (38/23 with complete data and successful sleep intervention) performed a cognitive reappraisal task during fMRI after a night of normal sleep and after restricted sleep (3 h). studies.title: Influence of repressive coping style on cortical activation during encoding of angry faces.
studies.abstract: Coping plays an important role for emotion regulation in threatening situations. The model of coping modes designates repression and sensitization as two independent coping styles. Repression consists of strategies that shield the individual from arousal. Sensitization indicates increased analysis of the environment in order to reduce uncertainty. According to the discontinuity hypothesis, repressors are sensitive to threat in the early stages of information processing. While repressors do not exhibit memory disturbances early on, they manifest weak memory for these stimuli later. This study investigates the discontinuity hypothesis using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

studies.title: fMRI investigation of response inhibition, emotion, impulsivity, and clinical high-risk behavior in adolescents.
studies.abstract: High-risk behavior in adolescents is associated with injury, mental health problems, and poor outcomes in later life. Improved understanding of the neurobiology of high-risk behavior and impulsivity shows promise for informing clinical treatment and prevention as well as policy to better address high-risk behavior. We recruited 21 adolescents (age 14-17) with a wide range of high-risk behavior tendencies, including medically high-risk participants recruited from psychiatric clinics. Risk tendencies were assessed using the Adolescent Risk Behavior Screen (ARBS). ARBS risk scores correlated highly (0.78) with impulsivity scores from the Barratt Impulsivity scale (BIS). Participants underwent 4.7 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) while performing an emotional Go/NoGo task. This task presented an aversive or neutral distractor image simultaneously with each Go or NoGo stimulus. Risk behavior and impulsivity tendencies exhibited similar but not identical associations with fMRI activation patterns in prefrontal brain regions. We interpret these results as reflecting differences in response inhibition, emotional stimulus processing, and emotion regulation in relation to participant risk behavior tendencies and impulsivity levels. studies.title: The neural correlates of regulating another person's emotions: an exploratory fMRI study.
studies.abstract: Studies investigating the neurophysiological basis of intrapersonal emotion regulation (control of one's own emotional experience) report that the frontal cortex exerts a modulatory effect on limbic structures such as the amygdala and insula. However, no imaging study to date has examined the neurophysiological processes involved in interpersonal emotion regulation, where the goal is explicitly to regulate another person's emotion. Twenty healthy participants (10 males) underwent fMRI while regulating their own or another person's emotions. Intrapersonal and interpersonal emotion regulation tasks recruited an overlapping network of brain regions including bilateral lateral frontal cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, and left temporo-parietal junction. Activations unique to the interpersonal condition suggest that both affective (emotional simulation) and cognitive (mentalizing) aspects of empathy may be involved in the process of interpersonal emotion regulation. These findings provide an initial insight into the neural correlates of regulating another person's emotions and may be relevant to understanding mental health issues that involve problems with social interaction.

studies.title: Down-regulation of amygdala activation with real-time fMRI neurofeedback in a healthy female sample.
studies.abstract: Psychiatric conditions of emotion dysregulation are often characterized by difficulties in regulating the activity of limbic regions such as the amygdala. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (rt-fMRI) allows to feedback brain activation and opens the possibility to establish a neurofeedback (NF) training of amygdala activation, e.g., for subjects suffering from emotion dysregulation. As a first step, we investigated whether feedback of the amygdala response to aversive scenes can improve down-regulation of amygdala activation. One group of healthy female participants received amygdala feedback (N = 16) and a control group was presented with feedback from a control region located in the basal ganglia [N(sum) = 32]. Subjects completed a one-session rt-fMRI-NF training where they viewed aversive pictures and received continuous visual feedback on brain activation (REGULATE condition). In a control condition, subjects were advised to respond naturally to aversive pictures (VIEW), and a neutral condition served as the non-affective control (NEUTRAL). In an adjacent run, subjects were presented with aversive pictures without feedback to test for transfer effects of learning. In a region of interest (ROI) analysis, the VIEW and the REGULATE conditions were contrasted to estimate brain regulation success. The ROI analysis was complemented by an exploratory analysis of activations at the whole-brain level. Both groups showed down-regulation of the amygdala response during training. Feedback from the amygdala but not from the control region was associated with down-regulation of the right amygdala in the transfer test. The whole-brain analysis did not detect significant group interactions. Results of the group whole-brain analyses are discussed. We present a proof-of-concept study using rt-fMRI-NF for amygdala down-regulation in the presence of aversive scenes. Results are in line with a potential benefit of NF training for amygdala regulation.

Sample is healthy females (eligible). The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Thus all inclusion criteria I5-I11 are met, and no exclusion criteria (E3–E7) apply. Full text appears complete.

studies.title: The role of arousal in the spontaneous regulation of emotions in healthy aging: a fMRI investigation.
studies.abstract: Despite ample support for enhanced affective well-being and emotional stability in healthy aging, the role of potentially important dimensions, such as the emotional arousal, has not been systematically investigated in neuroimaging studies. In addition, the few behavioral studies that examined effects of arousal have produced inconsistent findings. The present study manipulated the arousal of pictorial stimuli to test the hypothesis that preserved emotional functioning in aging is modulated by the level of arousal, and to identify the associated neural correlates. Young and older healthy participants were presented with negative and neutral pictures, which they rated for emotional content, while fMRI data were recorded. There were three main novel findings regarding the neural mechanisms underlying the processing of negative pictures with different levels of arousal in young and older adults. First, the common engagement of the right amygdala in young and older adults was driven by high arousing negative stimuli. Second, complementing an age-related reduction in the subjective ratings for low arousing negative pictures, there were opposing patterns of activity in the rostral/ventral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the amygdala, which showed increased vs. decreased responses, respectively, to low arousing negative pictures. Third, increased spontaneous activity in the ventral ACC/ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) in older adults was linked to reduced ratings for low arousing negative pictures. Overall, these findings advance our understanding of the neural correlates underlying processing of negative emotions with different levels of arousal in the context of enhanced emotional functioning in healthy aging. Notably, the results support the idea that older adults have emotion regulation networks chronically activated, in the absence of explicit induction of the goal to regulate emotions, and that this effect is specific to low arousing negative emotions.

studies.title: Neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in generalized anxiety disorder following mindfulness training.
studies.abstract: Mindfulness training aims to impact emotion regulation. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms can be successfully addressed through mindfulness-based interventions. This preliminary study is the first to investigate neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in GAD following mindfulness training. Furthermore, we compared brain activation between GAD patients and healthy participants at baseline. 26 patients with a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis were randomized to an 8-week Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR, N = 15) or a stress management education (SME, N = 11) active control program. 26 healthy participants were included for baseline comparisons. BOLD response was assessed with fMRI during affect labeling of angry and neutral facial expressions. At baseline, GAD patients showed higher amygdala activation than healthy participants in response to neutral, but not angry faces, suggesting that ambiguous stimuli reveal stronger reactivity in GAD patients. In patients, amygdala activation in response to neutral faces decreased following both interventions. BOLD response in ventrolateral prefrontal regions (VLPFC) showed greater increase in MBSR than SME participants. Functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions increased significantly pre- to post-intervention within the MBSR, but not SME group. Both, change in VLPFC activation and amygdala-prefrontal connectivity were correlated with change in Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) scores, suggesting clinical relevance of these changes. Amygdala-prefrontal connectivity turned from negative coupling (typically seen in down-regulation of emotions), to positive coupling; potentially suggesting a unique mechanism of mindfulness. Findings suggest that in GAD, mindfulness training leads to changes in fronto-limbic areas crucial for the regulation of emotion; these changes correspond with reported symptom improvements.

Abstract lacks key details: it does not state whether task-based fMRI was used, whether participants performed an explicit emotion regulation task, or whether task-related brain activation results are reported. Because inclusion cannot be determined from the abstract alone, include for full-text review to assess I1–I4.

The study is a task-based fMRI investigation of cognitive reappraisal vs passive viewing in healthy adults, reporting task-related neural activation and multivariate predictors of reappraisal success. It meets I1-I4 and no exclusion criteria are met.

Simultaneous EEG-fMRI in 20 human subjects during explicit emotion processing and regulation tasks; reports cortical activation and network results related to regulation. Meets I1-I4. No exclusion criteria identified in the abstract.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of human young adults performing cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) with task-related activation contrasts and results reported; does not meet any exclusion criteria. Full-text review appropriate to extract detailed activation data.

Exclude: study reports resting-state cerebellar-cerebral functional connectivity in OCD, not a task-based emotion regulation paradigm. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical sample). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related activation results).

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study using a reappraisal emotion-regulation task during scanning with human juvenile participants (clinical offenders and controls) and reports task-related brain activation differences. No exclusion criteria (non-empirical or irrelevant empathy-only tasks) apply.

Study is a structural MRI voxel-based morphometry study relating gray matter volumes to self-reported use of reappraisal and suppression, not a task-based fMRI experiment. Inclusion met: I3 (human young adult participants). Inclusion not met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). No exclusion criteria (E1,E2) apply.

Task-based fMRI study in human participants examining emotion regulation (implicit attention shift and appraisal) and reporting task-related brain activations; no exclusion criteria met in the abstract.

Abstract addresses neural correlates of negative emotions and emotion regulation during anticipation of difficult tasks, but it does not explicitly state that task-based fMRI was used, whether participants were instructed to regulate emotions (vs. natural responses), or report task-related brain activation results. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criteria from abstract alone; include for full-text review.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using a film-based emotion regulation task in human adolescents/young adults and presents task-related neural activation results (prefrontal cortex, amygdala). No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI in healthy adults reporting task-related brain activation. Abstract does not clearly indicate an instructed emotion-regulation task (primes implicitly modulate regulation), so I2 is uncertain; include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study using emotion regulation (reappraisal) in human participants and reports task-related activation (dorsolateral/ventrolateral PFC, cingulate). All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study including an explicit cognitive emotion regulation task and an emotional Stroop, includes patient and control groups, and reports task-related brain activation (left supramarginal gyrus). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal of aversive visual stimuli in human participants; reports task-related brain activation (amygdala, LPFC) and between-group comparison with/without neurofeedback. Meets all inclusion criteria; no exclusion criteria evident.

Task-based fMRI with participants viewing dental-treatment images that evoke fear/pain; reports task-related activation and connectivity in clinical and control groups. Abstract does not clearly state whether participants were instructed to regulate emotion (insufficient information). Because the review accepts studies that either regulate or simply view visual emotional stimuli, include for full-text review to confirm whether it meets the regulation-specific criteria.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in healthy participants and reports task-related brain activation, but does not clearly state that participants were instructed to regulate their emotional responses (uncertain whether it meets I2). Include for full-text review to determine if the mood induction involved explicit regulation instructions or comparable regulation strategies.

Study used structural (anatomical) MRI to measure dACC volume and trait emotion-regulation measures, not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation paradigm. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (healthy human participants). Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task), I4 (reports task-related brain activation).

Task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants (ages 6–23) reporting task-related brain activation and connectivity (amygdala, vmPFC, vlPFC). No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI with human participants (OD/BPD and healthy controls) performing an oddball task requiring attention amid negative emotional distractors (interpretable as cognitive control of emotion/affective regulation), and reporting task-related activation differences. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI in human participants (N=54, N=103) including two volitional reappraisal tasks (cognitive emotion regulation). Reports task-related group brain activation results and replicability metrics. No exclusion criteria met.

EXCLUDED: Study uses resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based emotion-regulation paradigm. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants; patient group with controls). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I2 (no emotion-regulation task), I4 (no task-related activation results).

Abstract reports a task-based pharmaco-fMRI study in humans using cognitive reappraisal of negative stimuli, with reported task-related activation and connectivity results; no exclusion criteria are met.

Excluding because the study used a reactive aggression provocation/retaliation task without instructing participants to regulate their emotional responses, so it does not meet I2. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (emotion regulation task not demonstrated). Exclusion criteria met: none.

E2 met: perspective-taking task without instructions to amplify or dampen participants' own emotional responses. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (unclear/no explicit emotion-regulation instructions or use of emotional visual stimuli).

Structural VBM study, not a task-based fMRI emotion regulation experiment. Inclusion met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion not met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related activation results). No exclusion criteria met (none).

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (up- and down-regulation) using visual stimuli (angry faces) in patients with depression and healthy controls; reports task-related neural activation (amygdala, insula, prefrontal regions). No exclusion criteria met.

Study is a task-based fMRI investigation of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human clinical (GAD, PD) and healthy control groups and reports brain activation results. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study examining emotion regulation and reports brain activation/connectivity in schizophrenia patients. It meets I1, I2, and I4. The abstract does not specify whether a separate control group was reported (I3 not demonstrated), but no exclusion criteria are met and information is insufficient to rule inclusion, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study with human participants instructed to use Compassion-meditation and Reappraisal to modulate emotional responses to film clips, and reports task-related brain activation. Thus meets I1,I2,I3,I4. No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract.

Task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) with human participants across ages; reports task-related brain activation (prefrontal, amygdala) and connectivity. No exclusion criteria are met.

No exclusion criteria met. The study uses resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) and self-report emotion regulation among adolescent inpatients, so I1 (task-based fMRI) is not met, I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task during stimuli) is not demonstrated, and I4 (task-related brain activation results) is not reported. I3 (human clinical adolescent sample) is met.

Excluded because the study used olfactory (odor) stimuli rather than the visual-stimuli required by this meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Exclusion criteria met: none (E1, E2 not applicable). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: does not meet the meta-analysis' stimulus-modality requirement (visual stimuli).

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants and reports task-related brain activation/effective connectivity (DCM) results. No exclusion criteria are met; inclusion criteria I1–I4 are satisfied based on the abstract.

No exclusion criteria met. I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), and I4 (task-related brain activation results) are reported. I2 (emotion-regulation task) is not met: the Cyberball social exclusion paradigm evokes emotion but participants were not instructed to regulate their responses.

Task-based fMRI study in human participants directly comparing reappraisal and distraction as emotion regulation strategies; reports subjective emotion ratings and task-related brain activation and functional connectivity (e.g., amygdala, prefrontal, parietal regions). Meets inclusion criteria for task-based fMRI, emotion regulation task, participant sample, and brain activation results.

Task-based fMRI in unmedicated depressed adults measuring pretreatment neural reactivity to emotional visual stimuli that predicts CBT response. This meets I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (clinical human participants), and I4 (reports task-related brain activation results). The abstract does not specify an explicit regulation instruction, but the review objective accepts viewing without regulating, so I2 is considered met. No exclusion criteria are identified from the abstract.

Task-based fMRI study of human participants using guided cognitive reappraisal (creative reappraisal) to regulate negative emotion; reports task-related brain activation (amygdala, hippocampus, ventral striatum). No exclusion criteria met based on abstract.

Study used arterial spin labeling at rest to examine correlations between habitual emotion regulation and baseline rCBF; it did not involve a task-based fMRI emotion regulation paradigm or report task-related activation. No exclusion criteria met.

No evidence participants performed an emotion-regulation task (I2 not met). Abstract describes passive viewing and rating of aversive/neutral scenes; reports task fMRI activations (I1, I4) in clinical and control groups (I3). No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports human fMRI results (amygdala reactivity and connectivity) in depressed vs control groups but does not specify an emotion-regulation task or passive viewing conditions. Inclusion uncertain from abstract alone — full text needed to confirm task type and whether it fits the meta-analysis definition of regulation/viewing.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal to regulate emotions during financial decisions (human participants) and reports task-related neural activation (amygdala, PFC, striatum). No exclusion criteria identified.

Task-based fMRI with human participants instructed to cognitively regulate responses to visual food stimuli (control urge to eat vs imagine consumption); reports task-related brain activation results in prefrontal and precuneus regions; meets I1, I2, I3, I4. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI with healthy human participants performing implicit (attentional control) and explicit (cognitive reappraisal) emotion regulation tasks; reports whole-brain task-related activation results. No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI with 21 healthy human participants performing emotion regulation strategies (mindfulness and suppression) in response to emotional visual stimuli; reports task-related brain activation results (amygdala attenuation and connectivity). Satisfies all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of human participants performing cognitive emotion regulation (CER) during aversive conditioning and reports task-related ventral striatal and network activation/results. This meets inclusion criteria I1–I4 and does not meet any exclusion criteria. Full text needed for details and contrasts for meta-analysis, so include for full-text review.

Study is a task-based fMRI investigation in humans using cognitive reappraisal of aversive images, reports vlPFC activity and subcortical pathway mapping linked to reappraisal success—i.e., task-related brain activation. No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports a task-based human fMRI study where participants used cognitive reappraisal to decrease negative emotions induced by bottom-up and top-down generation; neural (amygdala) and self-report results are reported, matching inclusion criteria for task fMRI, emotion regulation, participant groups, and task-related brain activation.

Task-based fMRI with human adolescent participants and task-related brain activation are clearly reported (I1, I3, I4). The abstract does not clearly state that participants were instructed to regulate their emotional responses (I2 uncertain)—it describes inhibitory control in presence of socioaffective cues, which may reflect cognitive control of emotion. Insufficient detail to determine whether this meets the review’s definition of an emotion regulation task, so include for full-text review.

Abstract indicates an empirical task-based fMRI study examining emotional reactivity and regulation in generalized anxiety disorder, reporting frontolimbic (prefrontal and amygdala) engagement. This fits I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I3 (clinical human participants), and I4 (task-related brain activation reported). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to confirm methods and control group details.

No exclusion criteria met. Excluded because the study uses resting-state fMRI (no task): it does not meet I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), or I4 (reports task-related activation). It does meet I3 (human participants of relevant ages). Based on the abstract, exclusion is clear.

FMRI component (Study 2) involved recalling negative autobiographical memories rather than regulating emotional responses to visual stimuli targeted by the meta-analysis objective. Inclusion met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Inclusion not demonstrated: fMRI regulation of responses to visual stimuli (meta-analysis target). No exclusion criteria met.

This is a structural MRI study of cortical gyrification, not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation study. Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (human clinical and matched control groups). Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related brain activation results).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in human participants performing an emotion regulation task (veterans with PTSD and controls), and reports task-related brain activation results (PFC, SMA changes). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to extract detailed task contrasts and results.

Task-based fMRI with adolescents performing an emotional attention task, reporting task-related brain activation. It is unclear whether participants were instructed to regulate emotions (I2 ambiguous), but the study fits the review objective (viewing or regulating). Include for full-text review to confirm I2 eligibility.

Excluded because the task used auditory stimuli (laughter perception), not visual stimuli required by the meta-analysis objective. Inclusion criteria met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criterion not demonstrated for this review: regulation of emotional response to visual stimuli (meta-analysis objective).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using an emotion-regulation task (cognitive reappraisal), with human participants (excess-weight and normal-weight controls), and reports task-related activation and connectivity results. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract reports an empirical task-based fMRI study of an emotion regulation (ER) task in human participants (n=60) and presents task-related neural activation changes pre- to post-training. No exclusion criteria are met.

fMRI study directly comparing cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression in human participants, examining neural bases — satisfies I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task: reappraisal and suppression), and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Human sample is implied, so I3 is met. No exclusion criteria (E1, E2) apply.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI not stated in abstract), I2 (no evidence participants performed an emotion-regulation task on visual stimuli—study involves mood induction and pain), I4 (task-related brain activation results not reported in abstract). Therefore excluded from this review.

Excluded: the study used resting-state fMRI and did not involve a task-based emotion-regulation paradigm. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related activation results). Confident the abstract lacks task-based emotion-regulation data and thus does not meet inclusion criteria.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI with reappraisal and acceptance emotion-regulation tasks in human participants (rMDD and controls), and reports task-related brain activation contrasts. No exclusion criteria evident from abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study comparing cognitive reappraisal and placebo emotion regulation, reports neural activation changes (amygdala, insula, PFC, subgenual cingulate), and involves human participants performing emotion regulation. Meets inclusion criteria I1–I4, and no exclusion criteria are evident. Include for full-text review to confirm details.

Study examines intrinsic brain activity/connectivity (resting-state) in obesity, not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation study. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related brain activation results).

Abstract reports investigation of neural correlates of emotion regulation in human participants (twins), satisfying I2 (emotion regulation task) and I3 (human participants). The abstract does not explicitly state use of task-based fMRI or report task-related activation results, so inclusion on abstract alone is uncertain; include for full-text review to confirm I1 and I4.

Study reports resting-state functional connectivity in bipolar disorder, not a task-based fMRI emotion regulation study. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical participants). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (no task-based fMRI), I2 (no emotion regulation task), I4 (no task-related activation reported).

No exclusion criteria were met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related activation/validation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 — abstract does not describe an emotion-regulation task (e.g., cognitive reappraisal or instructed regulation of emotional responses to visual stimuli); it focuses on DMN modulation/neurofeedback and DMN activation/deactivation tasks.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study examining volitional emotion regulation in veterans with PTSD and reports neural activation results. It does not clearly state whether a separate control group is included, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Study is a task-based fMRI with clinical and control groups and reports task-related brain activation. The abstract does not indicate participants were instructed to regulate emotions; stimuli were task-irrelevant and processed incidentally. Because it’s unclear whether this meets the review’s emotion-regulation or passive-viewing inclusion, include for full-text review to confirm.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in adult human participants that reports task-related brain activation (PFC and amygdala). The abstract meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are apparent, so include for full-text review.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of cognitive downregulation of negative/stressful sensations (emotion regulation), in human participants, and describes task-related brain activation results. Unclear whether stimuli were visual images specifically, so include for full-text review to confirm applicability to visual-stimulus meta-analysis.

Abstract states the study examined beliefs, practices, and the neural basis of emotion regulation but gives no methodological detail (e.g., whether task-based fMRI was used, nature of regulation task, or task-related activation results). Topic aligns with the review but abstract is insufficient to confirm I1–I4, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study of human participants using emotion regulation strategies (cognitive reappraisal and attention deployment) with reported task-related brain activation (amygdala, PFC). Meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3, and I4; no exclusion criteria are apparent from the abstract.

Study is resting-state functional connectivity, not a task-based emotion-regulation fMRI study. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task), I4 (reports task-related brain activation results). No exclusion criteria from E1/E2 are met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in humans using a social-emotional paradigm requiring control over automatic approach/avoidance actions (emotion regulation), reports task-related aPFC-amygdala activation in healthy police recruits; no exclusion criteria met.

EXCLUDED because inclusion criterion I1 (task-based fMRI) is not met: the study used fNIRS, not fMRI. Inclusion criteria met: I2 (emotion regulation/cognitive reappraisal task), I3 (human participants, adults), I4 (reports task-related brain activation results via PFC oxygenation). No exclusion criteria (E1,E2) are met.

Task-based rtfMRI neurofeedback in human participants that involves voluntary self-regulation of emotional (amygdala) activity with positive emotion induction and reports task-related connectivity/activation results; meets inclusion criteria I1–I4. No exclusion criteria met from abstract.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI of humans (young adult smokers) performing an emotion-regulation (distancing) task with visual cues; reports task-related brain activation results. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study assessing emotional reactivity and regulation paradigms and changes in brain function after therapy, which fits the review objective. The abstract does not state whether a separate control group is reported (I3 not demonstrated), so full-text review is needed to confirm. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI paradigm of face emotional processing with ICA showing components modulated by fear and possible implicit reappraisal, but does not state whether participants were instructed to regulate emotions or explicitly that subjects were human; insufficient detail to determine I2/I3—include for full-text review.

The study used an emotion-word Stroop to probe selective attention to emotional distraction, not an explicit emotion-regulation task (no instructions to up-/down-regulate or reappraise). Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human adult sample), I4 (task-related activation reported). Inclusion not met: I2 (emotion regulation task). No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in human adolescent girls using cognitive reappraisal (an emotion regulation task) and reports task-related DLPFC activation related to estradiol level. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply based on the abstract.

Task-based fMRI with human participants performing implicit emotion regulation (attention shifting and appraisal). Reports task-related brain activation in adults followed from childhood, matching the review objective and meeting inclusion criteria I1–I4. No exclusion criteria met.

The study is a task-based fMRI experiment using cognitive reappraisal to up- and down-regulate emotions during the Ultimatum Game, reports task-related brain activations, and involves human participants. No exclusion criteria apply.

fMRI task with human participants and task-related activation reported, but abstract does not clearly state participants were instructed to regulate emotion (reappraisal) — it reports recruitment of reappraisal-related regions during anticipation. Include for full-text review to determine if an explicit emotion-regulation task was used.

This is a task-based fMRI study (I1) with human participants (I3) reporting task-related activations (I4), but it does not involve an emotion-regulation task of emotional visual stimuli or instructions to regulate emotional responses (I2 not met).
EXCLUDED because inclusion criterion I1 (task-based fMRI) is not met: the study uses EEG rather than fMRI. Inclusion criteria met: I2, I3, I4. Exclusion criteria met: none (E1, E2 not applicable).

Task-based fMRI comparing two emotion regulation strategies (distraction and reappraisal) reporting decreases in negative affect and region-specific activation changes (amygdala, prefrontal, cingulate). Implies human participants performing regulation tasks and reports task-related brain activation. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI study of emotion regulation (worry induction and worry reappraisal) in late-life GAD reporting functional connectivity results; meets I1, I2, I3, and I4. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm sample/control details and task contrasts.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in humans that examined deliberate modification of emotional responses to negative stimuli (emotion regulation) in PTSD and trauma-exposed controls, and reports neural mechanisms—meeting I1-I4. No exclusion criteria apply.

The study examines regulation of negative autobiographical memories (internal recall), not regulation of emotional responses to visual stimuli required by the review objective. Inclusion criteria met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: none.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in healthy humans who performed an emotion regulation task (endogenous vs exogenous inhibition), and it reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is a task-based fMRI motor study of sequential finger movements, not an emotion-regulation task. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion not met: I2 (no emotion regulation/reappraisal). No exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports an event-related fMRI task (I1) in which human participants were instructed to increase, decrease, or not alter emotional responses to visual (positive/negative/neutral) pictures—i.e. cognitive emotion regulation (I2). Participants are human (I3) and the paper reports task-related brain activation results (prefrontal, amygdala) (I4). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of effortful emotion regulation (reappraisal) in bipolar disorder and reports altered prefrontal–amygdala effective connectivity. It meets I1, I2, and I4. Presence of a separate control group (I3) is not clearly stated, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study with human participants (24 women) performing cognitive reappraisal/social-distance emotion regulation; reports task-related brain activation (dmPFC, aPCC, amygdala) and peripheral measures. Meets inclusion I1–I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) using negative facial stimuli in healthy adult humans and reports task-related brain activation results (PFC, amygdala), meeting inclusion criteria; no exclusion criteria met.

Excluded because the abstract reports task-based fMRI (I1), human participants (I3), and task-related brain activation results (I4), but does not indicate an emotion-regulation task or instructions to modulate emotional responses (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met (E1/E2 not applicable).

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met / not demonstrated: I2 (participants performing an emotion-regulation task of visual stimuli as required by the review objective). Study uses thermal pain (non-visual) and manipulates perceived control rather than an explicit regulation task for visual emotional stimuli, so it does not address the review objective.

Study reports task-based fMRI in human participants performing cognitive reappraisal (watch vs reappraise) with clinical (SAD) and healthy control groups, and reports task-related brain activation/connectivity results. No exclusion criteria are met.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI not demonstrated — study reports structural MRI and resting-state fMRI), I2 (not an emotion-regulation task — Go/No-Go measures response inhibition, not regulation of emotional responses), I4 (no task-related brain activation results reported). Therefore exclude from this emotion-regulation task-based fMRI meta-analysis.

Study uses auditory stimuli (angry prosody) rather than visual stimuli required by the review objective, so it does not address the review's focus on regulation of visual emotions. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: regulation of visual stimuli (modality requirement).

Title/abstract indicate a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (an emotion regulation strategy) in human participants (girls at high risk for depression) and report neural activation; thus inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3, and I4 are met. No exclusion criteria are apparent from the abstract. Include for full-text review to extract activation contrasts and details.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical and control groups reported). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI study; structural MRI), I2 (no emotion regulation task reported), I4 (no task-related brain activation results). Study is structural MRI of volumes, so excluded from fMRI emotion-regulation meta-analysis.

Task-based fMRI comparing mindfulness and cognitive reappraisal during cued expectation and perception of negative images in healthy participants; reports task-related brain activation (medial PFC, amygdala, insula, caudate). All inclusion criteria I1–I4 are clearly met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI in human children/adolescents reporting task-related amygdala-prefrontal activation/connectivity and behavioral regulation. Abstract does not specify explicit instructed emotion-regulation strategy, but the study fits the review objective of viewing visual (maternal) stimuli that modulate emotion-related circuitry; inclusion of viewing-without-regulating studies is allowed. Full text needed to confirm task details and contrast definitions.

Exclusion IDs met: None. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants; pediatric PTSD sample). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Abstract describes structural cortical markers and structural brain substrates, with no mention of task-based fMRI or task activation, so the study does not meet the review inclusion criteria.

No evidence of task-based fMRI or task-related brain activation (I1 and I4 not met). Abstract describes diffusion MRI (fractional anisotropy) and behavioral/emotion outcomes in pediatric brain tumor survivors; no emotion regulation task is reported (I2 not demonstrated). Human participants with control group present (I3 met). No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) with clinical participants (GAD and PD) and reports task-related brain activations predicting CBT response. No exclusion criteria are met and inclusion criteria are satisfied.

Task-based fMRI study of human participants undergoing a social rejection paradigm reporting task-related brain activation. Abstract does not state an explicit emotion-regulation instruction (uncertain if fits I2), so include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in human participants (38 males) and reports task-related neural responses in emotion-regulation networks during virtual violent actions. It is unclear from the abstract whether participants were explicitly instructed to regulate their emotions (I2 not clearly demonstrated), so full-text is needed to confirm. I1, I3, and I4 are met based on the abstract; no exclusion criteria appear to apply.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (increase/decrease/maintain) of emotional responses to negative pictures in human participants and reports whole-brain BOLD activation results; meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is a resting-state rtfMRI neurofeedback training study, not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation experiment. (a) Exclusion IDs met: none. (b) Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). (c) Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported), I2 (emotion-regulation during a task or regulation of responses to visual stimuli not demonstrated).

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in human participants (low vs high externalizing psychopathology) reporting task-related brain activation (amygdala, parietal, occipital). Meets I1-I4 and does not meet any exclusion criteria. Include for full-text review.

Abstract describes reappraisal in internalizing psychopathologies with reported atypical frontal activity and brain–behavior relationships in human participants, implying task-related brain activation and an emotion regulation task. However, it does not explicitly state task-based fMRI or use of visual stimuli; full text needed to confirm I1. Include for full-text review to verify imaging modality and stimulus details.

Abstract reports a task using real-time fMRI (with simultaneous EEG) where participants learned volitional downregulation of amygdala BOLD via neurofeedback, leading to reduced amygdala reactivity to visual stimuli and improved implicit emotion regulation. These findings indicate task-related fMRI activation during an emotion-regulation task. Unclear whether regulation was performed specifically during stimulus presentation, so full-text review is recommended.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI of emotion regulation (cognitive reappraisal and distraction), healthy human participants, and reports task-related BOLD activation results. No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI with human participants and task-related activation reported (I1, I3, I4). Abstract does not clearly state that participants were instructed to regulate emotion (I2 not demonstrated), but the study may still be eligible for review because the meta-analysis accepts viewing without explicit regulation. Full-text needed to confirm whether an emotion-regulation instruction or relevant regulation-related paradigm was used.
